channel.title: ResearchBuzz - Transformed
channel.description: News and resources covering social media, search engines, databases, archives, and other such information collections. Since 1998.

item.title: This AI-Powered Archive Maps 115 Years of Swedish Political Advertising
item.description: Little Black Book: “​Propagandaindex is a new digital archive that brings together Swedish election posters from 1911 to the upcoming 2026 parliamentary election. It offers a new way to explore political communication, using AI-assisted analysis to reveal long-term patterns in the language, imagery and tone of more than a century of campaigning.”

item.title: Declassified CIA documents show clear warnings to presidents before 9/11
item.description: NBC News: “The documents, posted on the CIA’s website, cover the period from February 1998 to Sept. 12, 2001. All are drawn from the daily intelligence briefings that were given by the CIA and other spy agencies to Clinton and his successor, Bush…. The documents, which amount to more than 100 pages, show a steady stream of alarming but imprecise intelligence reports that bin Laden was preparing to attack the United States, either on U.S. soil or at embassies and U.S. military bases abroad. Many of them were heavily redacted.”

item.title: Matt Mullenweg tells (trolls?) Automattic staff, saying he’s back in control after CEO ouster
item.description: TechCrunch: “Matt Mullenweg has posted a message to Automattic’s Slack, claiming he is back in control as CEO of the WordPress.com parent company, according to a screenshot of the message seen by TechCrunch, which was confirmed by multiple employee sources.”

item.title: 10 Hacks Every Google Photos User Should Know
item.description: Lifehacker: “Google Photos doesn’t have to be one of those things that you set up and forget. Despite its initial simplicity, Google Photos is full of settings and features you can configure to make the app work better for you. With these hacks, you can manage a massive photo library, reduce cloud storage, hide pictures of your ex, and disable AI in search.”

item.title: 9/11 Changed the World in Many Ways. It Also Spawned the Digital Media Era
item.description: Vanity Fair: “Revisiting the observations I made back then, and since, it’s clear that subsequent advances in media and technology have changed how we disseminate, manipulate, and believe visual information—and how such breakthroughs have changed terrorism, war, the tactics of autocrats, and of those who oppose them.”

item.title: Never Forget, AI Slop Is Polluting 9/11 History on the Internet as We Speak
item.description: Gizmodo: “Welles Crowther became known as the Man in the Red Bandana after stories spread about his heroism on September 11, 2001. Now, an AI-generated image purporting to show Crowther rescuing people from the World Trade Center is going viral—the latest example of how fabricated images could distort our collective memory of 9/11 for generations.”

item.title: Cyberattack causes a flight delay? Airlines won’t owe you a hotel or meal
item.description: Cyberscoop: “Beginning next month, if a flight is canceled or delayed because of a cyberattack, feds will give airlines clearance not to hand out meal vouchers or hotels. The change is the result of a broader rule the Transportation Department published last week that establishes a new ’cause of delay’ category for tracking information, but that also reduces air carrier responsibilities to customers for 10 kinds of events.”

item.title: Hidden crypto farm in Mexican mountains puts spotlight on cartel funding
item.description: Reuters: “Crypto mining — which uses powerful computers to generate virtual assets such as bitcoin — represents a new frontier in Mexico’s fight against organized criminal groups, which have extended ​their reach beyond drug trafficking and extortion into the murkier realm of financial crime.”

item.title: English Museum to Repatriate Colonial-Era Human Remains
item.description: New York Times: “After years of negotiations, a British museum has agreed to return a colonial-era collection of human remains to the Indigenous Naga people of the Indian subcontinent, Naga representatives said on Saturday. The partial remains — a warrior’s cranium, a woman’s skull, a young person’s jaw and many others — have been far from home in the Pitt Rivers Museum at the University of Oxford for over 100 years.”

item.title: Mesa Verde National Park to return thousands of Native American artifacts and Indigenous remains to tribes
item.description: Denver Post: “Mesa Verde National Park plans to return more than 4,000 sacred Native American objects and the remains of 85 Indigenous people in its possession, marking the largest potential repatriation in the park’s recorded history.”

item.title: NASA Boosts Open Science, Data Sharing with Artemis Accords
item.description: NASA: “The science from every Moon rock sample, lunar dataset, and discovery produced through NASA’s Artemis program will be shared by the agency with the global scientific community. That commitment is upheld by all 71 countries that have signed the Artemis Accords, a set of principles for safe and transparent civil space exploration.” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: Egyptologist Fact-Checks AI’s Absolutely Insane Ancient Egypt
item.description: Geeks Are Sexy: “In this video, Egyptologist Professor Laurel Bestock takes on AI-generated ancient Egypt and points out just how much of it is completely wrong. From pyramids wearing giant golden hats to modern mirrors and pharaohs apparently running side hustles, AI has created a version of Egypt that feels more like a fever dream than history.”

item.title: Company looks to build data centers at fairgrounds across California, including Ventura County
item.description: Spectrum News: “[Rima Muna] and others urged the board to oppose an idea by Orange County based infrastructure company Global Stack. The company is looking to build a data-processing unit the size of a shipping container, a landing area for aircraft, and a parking garage at up to 70 fairgrounds across the state, including in Ventura County.”

item.title: Colorado’s largest data center to be built in Weld County after commissioners approve Global AI
item.description: Denver Post: “Weld County is set to become the home of Colorado’s largest data center after the commissioners approved a construction permit for Global AI. A day before the commissioners’ approval on Wednesday, the Greeley City Council already set in motion plans to annex the property.”

item.title: Teachers union reaches AI privacy deal with Microsoft
item.description: Politico: “The American Federation of Teachers and Microsoft have reached an agreement establishing privacy and safety protections for the use of artificial intelligence in schools.”

item.title: The Ivy League’s Surrender to AI Is Insane
item.description: Chronicle of Higher Education: “Are ‘students,’ in fact, anxious about AI? No. Students require no coaxing to hungrily explore AI’s potential. Those who are anxious about AI’s proliferation in education are the philosophers, literary scholars, engineers, biologists, and computer scientists warning that what’s going to render students professionally useless is not a dearth of AI practice but the lack of opportunities for serious AI-free learning. Whether these scholars need a ‘cure’ is something to be established, not assumed.”

item.title: OpenAI’s Sam Altman says it would be ‘ill-advised’ to go public in 2026
item.description: TechCrunch: “While OpenAI has filed confidentially for an IPO, the company will not be going public this year, according to CEO Sam Altman.”

item.title: Gov. Pillen Announces and Encourages Use of AI Chatbot on State Website, Nebraska.gov
item.description: Governor of Nebraska: “Governor Jim Pillen has announced the addition of a new feature on the state’s primary website – a resident-assistance chatbot. The Nebraska Navigator as it is known, went live on Sept. 1. Installation on the newly designed website marks the second phase of the AI chatbot project, which began as a pilot involving the Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV).”

item.title: San Francisco Mayor Declares Rent Emergency Amid A.I. Housing Frenzy
item.description: New York Times: “Mayor Daniel Lurie of San Francisco on Thursday declared a rent emergency and proposed several actions to combat evictions as residents face a deepening housing crisis amid the A.I. boom.”

item.title: Amazon’s Prime Video Is Using AI to Lip-Sync Actors’ Mouths in Dubbed Titles, Starting With German Series ‘Maxton Hall’
item.description: Variety: “Amazon‘s Prime Video is promising to make English-language dubs look more natural by using AI to sync up the way the actors’ mouths move on screen.”

item.title: Ingram’s AI Rollout Is a Success
item.description: Publishers Weekly: “Ingram Content Group began rolling out AI across its platforms in May 2025, and just 15 months later, the company’s chief commercial and content officer says it has transformed the way Ingram approaches metadata, advertising, and marketing, while helping accelerate the introduction of new services.”

item.title: Finland risks strained power supply after Google AI deal, opposition warns
item.description: Reuters: “Finland ​should introduce a national permitting system for data centres to prevent the risk ‌of power shortages and soaring energy prices, opposition parties said on Thursday following Google’s announcement of a large new investment in the country.”

item.title: Dallas garbage trucks are using AI cameras to flag code violations and give homes a “blight score”
item.description: TechSpot: “Want another reason why there’s a big pushback against artificial intelligence? In Dallas, AI-powered cameras mounted on trash collection trucks are photographing properties and assigning them a ‘blight score’ – a rating based on perceived code violations. NBC 5 obtained city records showing that Dallas started testing the AI cameras on bulk trash collection trucks in April, ramping up their use over the summer.”

item.title: AI Agents Are Now Emailing Me with Their Security Concerns
item.description: Schneier on Security: “I received the two emails below earlier in the month. They’re vaguely coherent. I suppose I shouldn’t be surprised that the corpus that AIs are training on contain data suggesting that I am someone to write to with random computer and network security problems. After all, I observe that behavior in many humans as well. (Hi, humans. Glad you’re still reading.)”

item.title: Moravian University Launches AI Lab to Model Ethical Innovation
item.description: Moravian University: “Moravian University announced the official launch of its AI Innovation Lab, a hands-on physical and collaborative space where students from any academic discipline can test ideas, learn emerging technologies, and build practical AI tools to address real-world challenges.”

item.title: Study Suggests AI-Generated Images Could Support Conservation, but Real-World Data Remains Essential
item.description: North Carolina State University: “New research finds there is no substitute for real-world observations, but that — under the right circumstances — AI-generated images can be used to improve the performance of computer models used for species identification and biodiversity monitoring.” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: 121 Blaugust posts
item.description: What The Fran: “I visited the Blaugust participants and these are my favourite blog posts from the second half of the month, following up from 132 Blaugust posts. A bunch of them are end of August wrap-up types because I’m always interested. Sadly I only read English so for the blogs in other languages I’ve tried to link something cool. Otherwise they, and other blogs that 404ed or didn’t have new posts, etc, are at the end of this list.”

item.title: The big winners and losers in U.S. website traffic over the past year
item.description: Search Engine Land: “Google Analytics 4 (GA4) became mandatory on July 1, 2023, when standard Universal Analytics properties stopped processing new data. Less than a year later, on May 14, 2024, Google began rolling out AI Overviews to U.S. users. The timing matters: The industry lost a clean, comparable measurement baseline just as search traffic patterns started to shift. So, over the past 12 months, who gained website traffic in the U.S., and who lost it?”

item.title: The search company that plants trees just launched a Linux browser to help Europe battle big tech
item.description: The Register: “Berlin-based eco-conscious search outfit Ecosia is expanding its range of European-focused web browsers to include a Linux version, citing the growing number of users in the EU looking for open alternatives to the clutches of American tech giants.”

item.title: Vimeo Can Decide To Change Your Plan and Force You to Pay 5x More
item.description: PetaPixel: “This new Studio subscription came to PetaPixel‘s attention because of a discussion on Threads, the origin of which has since been deleted for factual inaccuracies, about a huge Vimeo price hike. While some details weren’t quite correct, the basic complaint was: Vimeo determined the user was no longer eligible for an individual plan and needed to be moved to the new, much pricier Studio tier.”

item.title: Elon Musk threatens to sue over Gibney documentary’s “space lasers” claim
item.description: NPR: “Elon Musk has in recent days been targeting his ire at filmmaker Alex Gibney, whose forthcoming documentary, Musk, offers a scathing look at the tech mogul’s rise. Now, a lawyer for Musk is threatening to file a defamation lawsuit ahead of the film’s release next month.”

item.title: Scoop: TikTok rejects Meta ads amid settlement pressure campaign
item.description: Axios: “TikTok has rejected ads from Meta that call on TikTok and other tech platforms to join Meta in settling with U.S. state attorneys general in a landmark children’s safety lawsuit, sources told Axios…. Part of Meta’s historic multibillion-dollar settlement is contingent on its peers also agreeing to settle. Other tech firms have yet to publicly comment on their plans.”

item.title: Man Arrested After Showing Up at Police Station With a Truck Full of Flock Cameras
item.description: Gizmodo: “A New Mexico man, 44-year-old Jevon Martinez, took down 10 Flock camera systems himself on Wednesday, according to the Bernalillo County Sheriff’s Office (BCSO). Martinez livestreamed himself taking down at least one of the cameras, which he called ‘tyranny trees.’ In the stream, he also showed the back of his pickup truck filled with several other cameras.”

item.title: LinkedIn beats “BrowserGate” lawsuits over scanning users’ Chrome extensions
item.description: Ars Technica: “LinkedIn beat two lawsuits over its practice of scanning users’ browser extensions, with a judge granting the Microsoft subsidiary’s motion to dismiss the cases. The users who sued LinkedIn failed to adequately allege that they have standing to sue because neither asserted that they ‘had browser extensions installed that conveyed private information to LinkedIn,’ ruled Judge Vince Chhabria in US District Court for the Northern District of California.”

item.title: The secret knitting society designing blankets and clothing with data
item.description: Northeastern University: “Deep within the underbellies of online forums and social media sites, a global network of passionate knitters, crocheters, sewists and stitchers are quietly pioneering a bespoke form of data visualization, conveying complex statistical ideas through artistic handmade crafts.”

item.title: Heritage and Research Center begins archival work
item.description: The Observer: “The Heritage and Research Center has completed renovations along the Avenue and has begun receiving archival collections from 10 congregations — focusing on Catholic religious women. The center, which began as an idea discussed among congregations in 2018, is now transitioning from construction into the process of preserving, organizing and making the collections available to students, researchers and the public.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: archived by the Library of Congress
item.description: Today is 9/11. You don’t have to take my word for what I was doing 25 years ago today because it was I know some of y’all have been reading since 2001 or before. Thanks for sticking with me. Wishing everyone peace and comfort on this day.

item.title: Voters Are Asking A.I. About Elections. The Answers Can Vary by User.
item.description: New York Times: “Now the M.I.T. researchers are comparing how nearly a dozen large language models responded to a fixed group of questions about prominent midterm candidates and political issues. The team is also evaluating how the responses vary based on who claims to be asking (calibrating for gender, race, location or political leaning). For nearly a month so far, the researchers have regularly run automated sweeps of all the possible combinations of prompts and identities — 19,000 separate queries each time. They designed a public dashboard called the LLM Election Observatory for tracking how the A.I. models are responding.”

item.title: Indigenous Collections Care Guide
item.description: Discovered on LinkedIn: the “The Indigenous Collections Care Guide provides a framework to respect and recenter collections stewardship practices around the needs and knowledge of Native American and Indigenous community members.”

item.title: You can now plan IRL events on Snapchat
item.description: Engadget: “Snapchat is getting a very old-school social media feature: event planning. Called ‘Snapchat Plans’ the app is trying to foster IRL gatherings of its users with new tools to organize meetups of up to 200 people directly in the app.”

item.title: Google appears to be done with tablets, again
item.description: TechSpot: “It seems that Google has decided to call it a day when it comes to making tablets. Just three years after it was introduced, the Pixel Tablet, Google’s only remaining tablet model, has been removed from its store. The tech giant has erased its entire Tablets section from the storefront, so it appears we won’t see another Pixel Tablet from Google for a long time, if ever.”

item.title: What is JSONC and is it any better than JSON?
item.description: How-To Geek: “JSON has become a near-ubiquitous data format, used in API responses, save game files, and configuration. But many people feel it can be better, and various attempts have been made to expand or improve it. JSONC is one of those attempts.” Trailing commas in JSON have gotten me more than once.

item.title: I ditched online file converters for a Docker container with 1,000+ formats
item.description: MakeUseOf: “For the longest time, I’d relied on online file converters for all those quick conversion needs. As someone working with various types of media, I found an additional tab in my web browser convenient. However, I wouldn’t rely on these sketchy file-conversion websites nowadays, knowing the serious privacy concerns they pose. At the same time, I like the idea of opening a new tab to convert a file. A Docker container I came across recently, namely ConvertX, solved this problem for good!”

item.title: We’re living through an explainer epidemic
item.description: Dazed: “These days, there’s an explainer video for every topic you can imagine, and swarms of thinkfluencers – often armed with tiny mics – popping up left, right and centre. Some have a niche…. Others post their hottest takes in front of a green screen or sell DIY business strategies on Substack. Like everything on the internet, much of it is highly researched, and much of it is not – such is the nature of algorithmic culture, which rewards volume.”

item.title: Putin’s bot army is targeting German and French elections, Sweden warns
item.description: Politico: “Russia poses a threat to upcoming elections in Europe’s biggest democracies and social media platforms must ‘step up’ the fight against Moscow’s networks of bots, Sweden’s disinformation defense chief has warned.”

item.title: People Are Buying Facebook Beef to Avoid “Mystery Meat”
item.description: Playboy: “As a Chicagoan, ‘local beef’ usually refers to a fight with a neighbor over a parking spot, sports team, or hot dog condiments. Now, with food recalls happening seemingly every other day, reported government-sanctioned sales of wild horses to slaughterhouses, and President Donald Trump’s recent effort to lower beef prices, the term has taken on a more nutritious meaning. I never thought I would consider driving over an hour to buy ground beef on Facebook Marketplace, but in 2026, it sounds like a safer gamble than buying it on Amazon for $1.99 a pound.”

item.title: Nearly a decade after the Cambridge Analytica scandal, New Mexico alone is taking Facebook to trial
item.description: Associated Press: “Attorneys representing the state of New Mexico told jurors that targeted political ads, attempting to lower Democratic turnout during the 2016 election, used Facebook data sold to a political consulting firm, during opening statements in a trial over the platform’s data protections.”

item.title: Kentucky courts filing system part of ‘cybersecurity incident,’ judicial branch officials say
item.description: Ohio Capital Journal: “The Kentucky Administrative Office of the Courts said the system used for files for the Kentucky Supreme Court and Court of Appeals ‘experienced a cybersecurity incident.’ AOC said it was notified by the company Thomson Reuters Court Management Solutions about the incident within the company’s C-Track system files. The company said an unauthorized third party accessed and obtained court data from multiple states, including Kentucky Appellate Court data.”

item.title: Texas judge rules TikTok misled users on child safety feature
item.description: Reuters: “A Texas judge ruled on Thursday that TikTok violated the state’s consumer protection law by misleading users ​about how it filtered content for minors and ‌whether its ‘Restricted Mode’ feature shielded children from inappropriate material.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Forgotten no more: Search the stories of 12,500 Coastal Command heroes lost in WW2
item.description: BFBS Forces News: “The Coastal Command Losses Database was officially launched at the International Bomber Command Centre (IBCC) in Lincoln this week, bringing together what is believed to be the first truly comprehensive record of Coastal Command losses…. Described as the Royal Air Force’s ‘Cinderella Service’, it was often overlooked in favour of the better-known Bomber and Fighter Commands. Yet its work was fundamental to the Allied war effort, protecting vital sea lanes, hunting German U-boats, escorting Allied convoys and attacking enemy shipping.”

item.title: Michigan State Police opens new database for 200 cold cases
item.description: WZZM: “Michigan State Police (MSP) is launching a website highlighting unsolved crimes that have gone cold. September is National Cold Case Month and state police are hoping to bring attention to unresolved homicides, missing and unidentified persons and serial offenses.”

item.title: Google Search Introduces Live NFL Game Feed
item.description: MediaPost: “Google added a live National Football League game feed to search on Wednesday, allowing fans and spectators to follow along with game developments as they unfold on the field.”

item.title: TikTok is bringing voice notes to the comment section
item.description: Mashable: “TikTok’s comment section is about to get a lot more chaotic. The platform is rolling out a slate of new ways to interact beneath videos, including voice comments, polls, photo carousels, and Live Photos. The four new features expand what users can post beyond text and single image replies, giving TikTok’s famously active comment sections even more ways to become part of the content itself.”

item.title: Creatorverse: NFL Is Doubling Down on Creators as the US Open Struggles
item.description: The Wrap: “The NFL’s creator strategy has become a central part of its audience expansion efforts in recent years, especially as the NFL has made moves to expand its female and non-American audiences. Last year’s Creator of the Week program led to more than 86 million views across all YouTube and NFL channels. And this year creators are especially important as the NFL will have nine international games throughout the 2026-2027 season — the most in the league’s history.”

item.title: Ric Flair Suing FAM Networks, Claims He Was Duped By Influencer Talent Agency
item.description: Fightful: “Ric Flair is suing FAM Networks, an influencer talent agency that Flair claims duped him into signing away the rights to his own image and likeness while promising him a six-figure monthly revenue stream that allegedly never materialized.”

item.title: Macron urges EU ban on social media for under-15s in letter to Von der Leyen
item.description: Reuters: “French President Emmanuel Macron has urged the European Commission to back a European Union-wide ban on social media ​for children under 15 after France failed to enact its own legislation, his ‌office said on Tuesday.”

item.title: Australians will be able to switch off social media algorithms under planned legislation
item.description: BBC: “Australians would be able to switch off social media algorithms under draft legislation to be proposed this week. Communications Minister Anika Wells, who last year helmed the government’s world-first social media ban for under-16s, said the digital duty of care laws would ensure ‘some basic safety protections on an industry that hasn’t had to observe it’.”

item.title: Receipts, memes and supermarket shelves: how Iranians are documenting the economic cost of war online
item.description: The Conversation: “On Iranian social media, everyday items are being used to illustrate rampant inflation. Videos juxtapose the purchasing power of the same amount of money from one or two years ago with its current value. People capture supermarket shelves, photograph receipts, and make jokes about products that have become unaffordable for their households. These posts are more than just complaints about rising prices. Collectively, they are forming an unofficial cost-of-living diary of a nation under significant economic strain.”

item.title: UCF Researchers Receive NEH Grant to Preserve Noah Webster’s Dictionaries Online
item.description: University of Central Florida: “Researchers in UCF’s Department of English and Center for Humanities and Digital Research (CHDR) are slated to receive nearly $350,000 from the National Endowment for the Humanities (NEH) to create searchable digital editions of Webster’s historic dictionaries, giving scholars, educators and the public unprecedented access to foundational texts that helped shape American English.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: As Trump pushes for data centers, voters in key midterm races say they don’t want them
item.description: NBC News: “Dawn Vogel, a Republican county supervisor in rural Buchanan County, Iowa, doesn’t have a lot in common with the leading democratic socialists in Congress. But on this bit of policy they agree: Data centers are proliferating across the American landscape too fast.”

item.title: Robots protest rampant AI in Poland
item.description: AFP: “Around 30 robots marched through Warsaw on Monday, waving flags and ‘chanting’ slogans as part of an unusual protest calling for greater regulation of artificial intelligence and protections for workers threatened by automation.”

item.title: Malaysia’s data centres guzzling more power as temperatures soar, officials say
item.description: Reuters: “Malaysia’s data centres are consuming more power as temperatures rise, leaving a ​9 gigawatt gas-fired capacity gap for the government to fill by 2032, ‌officials said on Tuesday. The share of data centres in overall power consumption surged to a record 9.3% in the second week of August, compared with an average of 7% this year, Energy Commission ​CEO Siti Safinah Salleh said.” AI MODELS

item.title: Texas lawmakers attempt to track data centers’ water usage as state faces shortage
item.description: Spectrum Local News: “Saving water is paramount as Texas could face a fresh water shortage due to rapid population and industry growth. Many Texans are concerned about the amount of water data centers use for cooling and power generation as lawmakers try to track how much water the centers across the state use.”

item.title: Chicago has abundant water. Data center developers want a taste
item.description: Chicago Reader: “Waterways in Chicago and northern Illinois have supported industrial activity for more than a century, and now those same bodies of water are drawing an influx of proposed data centers that would tap into the region’s plentiful resources. These proposals have drawn considerable scrutiny, with experts and advocates concerned about the lack of transparency and public input in processes that govern the use of a public resource.”

item.title: The House Democrat who’s making AI regulation her No. 1 priority
item.description: Politico: “Rep. Lori Trahan’s decision last week to forgo a leadership bid to instead focus on developing artificial intelligence policy surprised some of her colleagues. It also left some of them wondering whether her thwarted attempt to work across the aisle on the subject was what doomed her prospects.”

item.title: Top employees for data center company eyeing Yellowstone County made matching political donations before announcing plans
item.description: Montana Free Press: “Two top executives from an out-of-state data center company made matching financial contributions to nine state political candidates in Montana the year before announcing plans to build in Yellowstone County.”

item.title: Data center nondisclosure bill dies in North Dakota Senate vote
item.description: North Dakota Monitor: “North Dakota legislators on Thursday rejected a push to ban the use of nondisclosure agreements between government entities and developers of data centers and other industrial projects. Bill sponsor Sen. Tim Mathern, D-Fargo, tried to persuade lawmakers that the bill was needed to preserve trust in government in the face of multi-billion dollar data center development projects that are popping up around the state.”

item.title: Massachusetts hits data centers with new clean power rules
item.description: TechCrunch: “Massachusetts became the latest state to force data centers to bring their own power, but this time there’s a twist. A new state mandate would require developers building data centers larger than 25 megawatts to provide clean power or pay into a ratepayer protection fund. Gov. Maura Healey’s executive order is the latest example of states turning against data centers.”

item.title: Lawmakers propose oversight for state, local agencies using AI
item.description: Nevada Current: “Concerned that Nevada agencies have relied on artificial intelligence without much oversight, state lawmakers are proposing legislation to establish basic standards on how the technology is used by state and local government entities. Proposed legislation that would require transparency around AI and prevent bias in automated decision making was among the nine bill draft requests approved at the Aug. 27 the interim Government Affairs Committee meeting.”

item.title: DeepSeek embarks on ‘unprecedented’ hiring spree as it overhauls back end systems
item.description: South China Morning Post: “Chinese artificial intelligence start-up DeepSeek is embarking on what it calls an ‘unprecedented’ hiring spree to overhaul back end systems severely strained by booming user demand and compute-heavy AI agents.”

item.title: Nvidia’s Hugging Face purchase confirmed at $13 billion
item.description: Mashable: “It’s official: Nvidia has acquired the open-source AI platform Hugging Face for $13 billion. Or, according to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, the acquisition was for $12,930,300,000, to be exact.”

item.title: AI deepfakes and fake fighters reshape Mali’s information war
item.description: RFI: “Mali’s warring sides are increasingly using artificial intelligence to fight an information war alongside their battle on the ground, a study published Wednesday has found. Jihadists are experimenting with relatively basic AI propaganda, separatist networks are creating fake online characters and Russia’s Africa Corps is using the technology on a far more sophisticated scale.”

item.title: Fact check: Is Sam Altman right that almonds use more water than ChatGPT queries?
item.description: Cal Matters: “On the Sources Podcast with Alex Heath released Tuesday, Altman said that it takes 38,000 ChatGPT queries to use as much water as producing a single almond in California. ‘If you look at a modern very large data center, it uses the equivalent amount of water as an office building in terms of, you know, people like running the sinks and the toilets and whatever,’ Altman told Heath. The problem, experts say, is that it’s impossible to verify those numbers given what’s public about the secretive industry.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: USGS Cooperative National Geologic Map Now Covers 50 States, U.S. Territories
item.description: USGS: “This version is the first digital map to provide standardized geologic data for all 50 states and most territories. Through the innovative map interface developed by the USGS National Geologic Map Database, anyone can view and interact with the map data to learn more about the Nation’s geologic framework, resources, and hazards.”

item.title: Tracking Censorship in National Parks: An Update from the Save Our Signs team
item.description: Data Rescue Project: “As censorship of NPS materials continues, the Save Our Signs team has released new resources and a key update to the existing infrastructure to make it easier to understand what has changed.”

item.title: Automattic’s board forces CEO Matt Mullenweg into leave of absence
item.description: TechCrunch: “Matt Mullenweg, the founder and CEO of Automattic, best known as the parent company of WordPress.com, has been put on a leave of absence by his board against his will, according to a Slack message seen by TechCrunch.”

item.title: 60 Posts in 10 Hours: How Trump’s Social Media Reflects His Version of Reality
item.description: New York Times: “The rat-a-tat of ever wilder, ever more outrageous posts each weekend has become a fixture of the president’s second term, seen more and more as a barometer of his mental state. Mr. Trump’s critics, who never considered him a model of stability in the first place, now point to these frenetic bursts of fantasy and vanity as proof that the 80-year-old president is deteriorating further with age.”

item.title: GOG brings back “big box” PC games, one printable template at a time
item.description: Ars Technica: “Those who remember PC gaming in the days before Steam may have fond memories of the ‘big box’ packaging that made those games stand out as shelf eye candy and sought-after in-home collectibles. Today, PC gaming platform GOG is hoping to reignite some of the nostalgia for those days by adding downloadable 3D models and printable, foldable high-res packaging scans for a handful of PC games on the platform.”

item.title: Are 200 million LG TVs listening in – even when switched off?
item.description: Cybernews: “LG smart TVs can listen in on voice commands, gather data that reveals your location, and scan your home for other connected devices, according to a major new investigation into the company’s webOS platform.”

item.title: Meta Fails To Remove Sex Abuse Ads Featuring Real Children
item.description: MediaPost: “Last month, an investigation led by the Tech Transparency Project (TTP) found that Meta had been running dozens of paid ads including explicit AI-generated CSAM material targeting users living in the U.S. and Europe. Some of the ads invited users to link to AI-powered undressing apps. According to Meta’s ad library, the CSAM ads were running across Facebook, Instagram, Messenger, and Threads.”

item.title: What does it look like to create an ethical visual archive that’s truly accountable to the community it documents?
item.description: University of Minnesota: “Ethical documentary work cannot begin with cameras or interview questions; it begins with listening, trust, and understanding a community’s priorities. I learned this lesson while interning with Soomaal House of Art, a Minnesota-based Somali artists collective, when the direction of the project I worked on this summer changed because Kaamil Haider, co-director and co-founder of Soomaal House of Art, and I listened to the collective’s needs, not only my initial expectations, to guide our work.”

item.title: Trump Officials Remove Military Language Critical of the Confederacy from Memorial Site
item.description: People: “The Trump administration has removed language from Arlington National Cemetery that was critical of a Confederate memorial that was taken down in 2023. The changes were made to both a marker at the memorial’s former location and a Department of Defense (DoD) website that provided historical context about the monument.”

item.title: Health officials turn to mobile-phone data to track Ebola spread in Congo
item.description: Reuters: “Health officials battling the Ebola outbreak in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo are using anonymised mobile-phone data to map population movements and identify areas where the virus could ​spread next, according to the World Health Organisation and researchers working with it. The approach, which has not been used before in an Ebola response, comes as authorities struggle ‌to contain what the WHO has described as the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record.”

item.title: The Majesty of Birds Celebrated in the 2026 Audubon Photography Awards
item.description: PetaPixel: “The National Audubon Society has unveiled the winners of the 2026 Audubon Photography Awards, a competition that captures the beauty of birds and the challenges they face. The competition, now in its seventeenth year, is split into two geographic areas: Chile and Colombia, as well as the United States and Canada. This is to highlight ‘how birds connect people across geographies and ecosystems.'” Good morning, Internet…

item.description: Mogura VR: “The oldest theater in the Kinki region, ‘Izushi Eirakukan,’ has been digitally archived using 3D scanning, making it accessible via VRChat and other virtual reality platforms.”

item.title: After 9/11, Documents Suggest, New Yorkers Were Misled About Air Quality
item.description: New York Times: “The Mamdani administration released more than 170,000 pages of documents related to the air quality around the World Trade Center site in the months after the Sept. 11 attacks.”

item.title: New Mexico immigrant advocates launch platform for training, job opportunities amid federal threats
item.description: Source NM: “Somos Un Pueblo Unido, a New Mexico immigrant advocacy organization, on Thursday launched an online platform seeking to connect foreign-born residents with a variety of state workforce development programs aimed at connecting workers with industries that need them.”

item.title: Tate brothers lose bid for release from US jail pending extradition
item.description: Reuters: “Social media influencers Andrew ​and Tristan Tate lost their bid for release from a Miami jail on Wednesday as they contest extradition to Britain, where ‌they are wanted on rape charges. In denying bail for the Tate brothers, Miami-based U.S. Magistrate Judge Lauren Louis said the brothers’ wealth and frequent international travel made them ‘quintessential flight risks.'”

item.title: Audacity’s new look is finally here, along with its largest feature update in years
item.description: Engadget: “Audacity released its Version 4.0 update today, bringing a fresh coat of paint and a number of new features for the popular free and open-source audio editor. This is the biggest update since Version 3.0 caused a ruckus over five years ago, and users have been waiting to see how radically the software would change with this latest release.”

item.title: The 15th Anniversary of TCMParty
item.description: A Shroud of Thoughts: “Today TCMParty turns 15 years old. For those of you who do not know what TCMParty is, it is a collective live posting of movies on Turner Classic Movies using the hashtag #TCMParty. It originated on Twitter and has since largely moved to Bluesky, although the hashtag is used on other social media services as well. Originally, TCMParties were scheduled and had hosts who posted trivia about the specific movie then airing. The hosts essentially curated the live posting. While scheduled TCMParties with a host still take place, TCMParty has evolved to where it takes place 24 hours a day.”

item.title: FCC plans robocall scorecard to grade phone companies on spam call blocking
item.description: Ars Technica: “The Federal Communications Commission today said it will create a robocall mitigation scorecard to rate phone companies on how effectively they block illegal spam calls.”

item.title: Grindr pays £26m to settle UK lawsuit over allegedly sharing users’ HIV status
item.description: The Guardian: “Grindr will pay £26m to settle a lawsuit brought by thousands of users in the UK who allege that the US dating app shared highly sensitive personal information, including in some cases their HIV status, with advertising companies.”

item.title: Medieval Manuscripts Reveal DNA of a Deadly Livestock Disease
item.description: Medievalists.net: “Medieval manuscripts have preserved much more than the words written on their pages. Scientists examining the animal skins used to make books such as the 1,000-year-old York Gospels have discovered DNA from sheeppox, revealing that the devastating livestock disease was circulating across medieval Europe.”

item.title: Defrag98
item.description: Spotted in my RSS feeds: , a Windows 98 defrag simulation. I would be very concerned if my hard drive had ever sounded like this simulation, but I like the defrag part. Good evening, Internet…

item.title: Tariff confusion
item.description: Centre For Economic Policy Research: “We construct the new US Tariff Announcement Database (USTAD), which tracks US tariff announcements during 2025. We use USTAD to compute monthly US statutory tariffs and novel measures of tariff confusion by origin country and product: the number of relevant announcements, the number of possible tariff calculations arising, and bounds on possible tariff miscalculation. We find that confusion about the current state of US tariff policy led to significant declines in US imports during 2025. Strikingly, we estimate that the fall in US imports due to tariff confusion was similar in size to the reduction caused by tariff increases alone, meaning that confusion doubled the negative impact of tariffs.”

item.title: BET.com Article Explorer
item.description: Spotted on Bluesky: the From the About page: “In September 2026, BET removed its news archive from bet.com — more than two decades of reporting on Black culture, politics, music and public life, gone from the live web. The articles themselves survived, because the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine had been capturing them all along. This site makes those captures searchable again.”

item.title: Nitter lives to proxy another day after taking legal advice
item.description: The Register: “The Nitter project will continue ‘following legal advice,’ meaning XCancel, a public service built on its open source code, is back online.”

item.title: Dismantling Disinformation
item.description: American Libraries: “Library workers are well aware of the effects of book bans and censorship. Propaganda and disinformation are the flipside of the same coin. Understanding the complex relationships among these interrelated processes is more critical than ever, especially as libraries explore possible solutions and responses. The following books show how disinformation can lead to censorship and how censorship can, in turn, allow disinformation to thrive.”

item.title: Social Media Dog Tucker Budzyn Dies Days After Owner Announced the Golden Retriever’s Cancer Diagnosis
item.description: People: “Tucker Budzyn, the beloved viral golden retriever, has died following complications from cancer. He was 8 years old. His owner, influencer Courtney Budzyn, announced the news in a tearful video on Saturday, Sept. 5, sharing that Tucker died on Wednesday, Sept. 2 — less than a week after she revealed his lymphoma diagnosis.” When I was looking after my Granny during Covid, I would find YouTube videos I thought she’d like and bring them over for her to watch. She loved dogs and Tucker was a big favorite. Granny died December 17 of last year and now Tucker is gone.

item.title: Why this month’s Microsoft patch release is a doozy
item.description: Ars Technica: “Microsoft’s patch for September is a doozy, with a record number of roughly 972 vulnerabilities fixed and 112 of them meeting the high critical-severity threshold. It was only two months ago that Microsoft patched a then-record 570 vulnerabilities. Then, last month, Microsoft patched some 620 of them. Google and other companies have also published record numbers of vulnerabilities in recent months.”

item.title: YouTube has blocked the channels of Kirkorov, Povaliy, and other propagandists
item.description: UA.news: “The list includes channels belonging to Philip Kirkorov, Grigory Leps, Sergey Lazarev, Valeria, Larisa Dolina, Irina Allegrova, and the band ‘Pelageya.’ Access has also been restricted to the channels of Denis Maidanov and Yulia Chicherina, who support Russia’s aggression against Ukraine.”

item.title: New evidence shows Boulder climate lab was dismantled in act of political reprisal, lawsuit alleges
item.description: Colorado Sun: “New evidence shows overt political retaliation against Colorado is behind the Trump administration’s dismantling of the National Center for Atmospheric Research lab in Boulder, according to new filings in a lawsuit by the lab’s university consortium managers.”

item.title: Decades after colonial-era mapping, Africa’s mineral powerhouse launches $180 million drive with US, France, others to control mineral data
item.description: Business Insider Africa: “The push comes decades after Belgian authorities and mining companies conducted extensive geological surveys across the territory during the colonial era. Much of that information remains outside the DRC, including millions of pages of maps, field notes and geological records stored at Belgium’s AfricaMuseum in Tervuren…. The historical data has taken on new importance as the DRC sits at the centre of the global race for critical minerals, particularly copper and cobalt.”

item.title: New Guidelines Created for Publishing Indigenous Data
item.description: Dartmouth College: “To ensure that Indigenous peoples’ rights and knowledge are recognized in scientific data and scholarly publishing, a team of Indigenous scholars led by Lydia Jennings, an assistant professor of environmental studies, has established Guidelines for the Governance of Indigenous Peoples’ Data in Scholarly Publishing.”

item.title: This New Open-Source Camera Has Swappable Sensors and Lens Mounts
item.description: PetaPixel: “CHC5 modules start at under $200 for backers, and the camera base itself, with a sensor and mount of choice, is around $680. The system is entirely open-source, rendering it easy to customize for even niche applications. With interchangeable sensors mounted on uniform boards, swappable lens mounts, and open-source software, the potential imaging applications are expansive.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: National Summit on Local News Preservation Report
item.description: Internet Archive Blog: “On June 17, 2026, the Internet Archive hosted the National Summit on Local News Preservation in National Harbor, Maryland. Organized through our Today’s News for Tomorrow (TNT) program with partners the Poynter Institute and Investigative Reporters and Editors (IRE), and with support from Press Forward and the Society of American Archivists Foundation, the Summit brought journalists, librarians, archivists, and researchers into the same room…. The TNT Project Team has released a report documenting the proceedings of the Summit and offering recommendations. The report also provides an analysis of breakout group discussions and identifies areas for future action.”

item.title: White House Removes Awful Tetris Clone From Website After The Tetris Company Posted It Takes ‘Copyright Infringement Very Seriously’
item.description: Kotaku: “The White House has quietly removed a racist and not-very-well-made Tetris clone from its awful ‘arcade’ website. The move comes shortly after The Tetris Company publicly criticize the clone while reminding everyone that it has a history of going after clones and knock-offs in court.”

item.title: Google complies with EU rules for travel searches, says the new results stink
item.description: Ars Technica: “As the world’s largest search engine, Google is often a target of Europe’s Digital Markets Act (DMA), which seeks to rein in Big Tech. The European Commission hit Google with a hefty 460 million euro ($543 million) fine in July for preferring its own services in searches for travel and shopping. Google has now made changes in accordance with the European Union’s wishes, but it claims the result is a massive reduction in search quality.”

item.title: Can Evan Spiegel Sell the World on $2,195 Smart Glasses?
item.description: Wall Street Journal: “Snap CEO Evan Spiegel bet big on developing new smartglasses and was ready to show them to the world. But as Spiegel prepared for a CNBC interview in June ahead of the fall product launch, at least one person internally advised him not to wear the glasses for the entire segment and instead focus on talking about them, according to people familiar with the matter. Spiegel wore them anyway.”

item.title: Fujifilm and Google Launch New Google Photos Print Store
item.description: PetaPixel: “Fujifilm has announced “Fujifilm for Google Photos Print Store,” a new print storefront that brings physical photo printing to Google Photos users. Fujifilm says it ‘will assume leadership and responsibility for the photo printing functionality of the popular Google Photos platforms,’ and plans to release new features and products to improve the overall Google Photos user experience.”

item.title: Fake Version of Republican Midterm Convention Website Redirects to Epstein Files
item.description: New York Times: “Republicans eager to find out more about the party’s first-of-its-kind midterm convention in Dallas next week got a surprise this week: a website that initially purported to be the Republican National Committee’s official convention page but then redirected to the Justice Department’s library of files related to Jeffrey Epstein, the convicted sex offender.”

item.title: YouTuber Jack Doherty arrested on domestic battery charge in Fort Lauderdale
item.description: Local10: “Fort Lauderdale police said they arrested the 22-year-old after a ‘domestic dispute’ late Friday morning in the city’s Riverside Park neighborhood. Authorities said officers responded to the 1400 block of Southwest Fifth Court just before noon and determined that Doherty ‘and a female victim got into a physical dispute inside a residence.'”

item.title: Party’s over for crypto scammers who went on a spending spree after a $240 million bitcoin theft
item.description: Associated Press: “The scammers — a network of young men in their late teens or early 20s — celebrated the August 2024 heist by embarking on a wild spending spree. They purchased fleets of sports cars, flew on private jets, hired security guards and rented mansions in Miami and the Hamptons. An alleged ringleader, 22-year-old Malone Lam, spent over $569,000 in one evening at a Los Angeles night club. Their bender lasted a month before FBI agents arrested Lam on charges that he organized a ‘social engineering’ attack on the Washington, D.C., resident. ”

item.title: Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch is leaving amid tensions with Trump
item.description: NBC News: “While the Smithsonian has traditionally operated independently of the party in power, the Trump administration has repeatedly criticized how the institution portrays America’s past. Last week, the Interior Department threatened to cut off support, alleging that Smithsonian facilities present a ‘radical ideology’ that weakens ‘shared American identity.'”

item.title: ‘Insane data’: Duke professor Dan Ariely accused of additional research fraud
item.description: Duke Chronicle: “Dan Ariely, professor of business administration in the Fuqua School of Business, is once again under scrutiny after an article released Monday found evidence that he likely tampered with or fabricated data in an influential 2002 research paper on procrastination.” Good evening, Internet…
